item.title: Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor [1] (ICLR 2026), Stefan Nielsen, Edoardo Cetin, Peter Schwendeman, Qi Sun, Jinglue Xu, and Yujin Tang (Sakana AI, University of Michigan, and Institute of Science Tokyo) train a 7B conductor with reinforcement learning to plan how a pool of LLMs should talk to each other and what to tell each one, and then let it call itself recursively to spend more compute on hard queries.

Powerful large language models (LLMs) from different providers have been expensively trained and finetuned to specialize across varying domains. In this work, we introduce a new kind of Conductor model trained with reinforcement learning to automatically discover powerful coordination strategies among LLMs. Our Conductor learns not only to design targeted communication topologies for effective agent-to-agent collaboration, but also to prompt engineer focused instructions to the LLMs to maximally leverage their individual capabilities. We show that, by learning optimal coordination strategies over pools of powerful worker LLMs, a 7B Conductor achieves significant performance gains beyond any individual worker, attaining state-of-the-art results in challenging reasoning benchmarks, such as LiveCodeBench and GPQA. By training with randomized agent pools, our conductor effectively adapts to arbitrary sets of open- and closed-source agents, meeting any user requirements. Furthermore, allowing the Conductor to select itself as a worker gives rise to recursive topologies, elevating performance with a new form of dynamic test-time scaling through online iterative adaptation. More broadly, ours is among the early work demonstrating language model coordination can be unlocked through RL, where powerful coordination strategies emerge naturally in LLMs through pure end-to-end reward maximization.

Methods

The Conductor is itself an LLM, a 7B model finetuned from a Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoint [2], with no architectural change to the transformer. The novelty is not the model but what it is trained to output: instead of answering a query, it emits a complete agentic workflow in natural language, which an outer loop then executes by calling the worker models.

What the Conductor outputs

  • The output is a parsed workflow. After its chain-of-thought, the Conductor emits up to five workflow steps as three aligned Python lists: the natural-language subtask for each step, the integer id of the worker assigned to it, and an access list naming which earlier steps’ outputs that worker may see. The harness parses these lists and runs the steps in order, prompting each named worker with its subtask plus only the prior responses its access list grants. The Conductor produces no answer content of its own.
  • Natural language as the output medium is the design choice. Prior multi-agent routers pick from a set of pre-specified topologies. Emitting the workflow as free-form text instead gives what the authors call complete specification freedom, letting one model express best-of-N, sequential chains, or arbitrary parallel trees within the same format. Both halves of an agentic step, which worker to call and what exact instruction it gets, are learned jointly, so the Conductor does prompt engineering rather than only routing.

How it is trained

  • End-to-end with GRPO on the executed workflow’s reward. Training uses GRPO [3] with a two-part reward: 0 if the three lists can’t be parsed, then 1 if the executed workflow’s final output matches the ground-truth solution and 0.5 otherwise. The signal comes only from running the whole plan to completion, with no supervised labels for who-should-do-what. From that single reward the authors observe problem breakdowns, worker-matched instructions, and communication topologies emerge on their own.
  • The training set is 960 deliberately-hard problems. The Conductor trains on 960 problems across four domains: MATH500 [4] (math), MMLU [5] (multitask knowledge), LiveCodeBench [6] (code), and RLPR [7] (general reasoning). The authors pick the harder variants of benchmarks common in multi-agent work, using AIME-style difficulty over GSM8K [8] and pairing LiveCodeBench’s oldest version for training with its newest for testing, which guards against contamination.
  • Randomized agent pools during training. The available worker set is resampled at each training step, so the Conductor learns to coordinate arbitrary mixes of open and closed models rather than memorizing one fixed roster. At test time a user can hand it any pool, including one with no paid API calls.

Recursion at test time

  • Recursive self-calls buy more test-time compute. Letting the Conductor name itself as a worker produces recursive topologies: an inner call receives its parent’s output together with the previous agent’s response. Recursion is unlocked by a short finetune that instantiates one recursion call for half the samples in each batch, and is capped at a maximum depth. Spending more recursive depth raises accuracy on hard queries.

Results

The Conductor is evaluated in-domain on held-out questions from its four training tasks and out-of-domain on AIME 2025 [9], BigCodeBench [10], and GPQA-Diamond [11]. Baselines include the strongest single models (Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and several open models), multi-agent methods (Mixture-of-Agents [12], MASRouter [13], Smoothie [14], RouterDC [15]), and single-model self-reflection, with cost tracked as the average number of model calls per query.

Accuracy

  • Beats each pool member alone, averaged across seven tasks. The 7B Conductor averages 77.27 across the four in-domain and three out-of-domain tasks, ahead of GPT-5 (74.78), Gemini 2.5 Pro (70.97), and Claude Sonnet 4 (65.69), and it sets the best score on GPQA-Diamond (87.5) and LiveCodeBench (83.93) [1]. These single models are the Conductor’s own workers, so the comparison pits the orchestrated pool against each member run alone rather than against an outside frontier. The gain comes from routing and composing models the Conductor already has, with no added capability of its own.

Cost efficiency

  • Beats multi-agent baselines at a fraction of the cost. Averaged across tasks the Conductor lands above Mixture-of-Agents, Smoothie, MASRouter, and RouterDC while making far fewer calls, roughly three per query against Mixture-of-Agents’ eight (Figure 5) [1].

Scaling and adaptivity

  • The 7B’s edge over the 3B is better instructions. A 3B Conductor already learns to concentrate calls on the three strongest models, and scaling to 7B adds further gains even when the agent selection is held fixed, which the authors attribute to better-written instructions. The Conductor also matches compute to difficulty, using two agents on MMLU and three or four on LiveCodeBench.

My Notes

  • RL works here, where Trinity’s did not. The Conductor trains a coordinator with reinforcement learning, while the sibling Trinity [16] found REINFORCE too low-signal to learn from and switched to an evolutionary strategy. The split is scale and action space: the Conductor is a full 7B model emitting natural-language topologies and prompts, a rich space reward signals can shape, whereas Trinity optimized a ~10K-parameter head over a discrete pick-a-model-and-role choice. The two papers map opposite corners of the same coordinator-training problem, and Sakana ships both as separate models behind one endpoint in Sakana Fugu [17]: the quality-first Fugu-Ultra builds on the Conductor, while the everyday Fugu builds on Trinity. They are not two stages of one orchestrator.
  • Recursion beats reflection as a scaling knob. A self-reflection loop re-runs one model on its own output. The Conductor’s recursive self-call instead re-plans the whole topology with fresh instructions, and it shifts toward the strongest workers (Claude and Gemini) in deeper rounds. That makes recursion depth a compute dial the user can turn up, and it is the mechanism Sakana Fugu [17] later exposes as its higher-effort Fugu-Ultra tier.
  • Accuracy reported per call. Most multi-agent papers report only accuracy. The Conductor’s Figure 5 puts accuracy against average model calls, and its win arrives at roughly three calls against Mixture-of-Agents’ eight. This is the economy the triager pattern chases from the cost side, escalating only when needed, reached here by learning when fewer agents suffice. MAPO [18] trains a closely related decision about when to defer.
  • The pool sets the ceiling. The single models the Conductor beats are its own workers, so the result measures the orchestrated pool against each member alone rather than against an outside frontier. The 7B adds no answer capability of its own. On AIME, where GPT-5 is already the best worker, the paper says the full-pool Conductor only matches its own GPT-5-only variant, which bounds the gain: orchestration helps when the right answer is split across different models, and reduces to picking the single best worker when one model already dominates. This is the same limit Trinity [16] hits against its per-question-best oracle.

item.title: TRINITY: An Evolved LLM Coordinator
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In TRINITY: An Evolved LLM Coordinator [1] (ICLR 2026), Jinglue Xu, Qi Sun, Peter Schwendeman, Stefan Nielsen, Edoardo Cetin, and Yujin Tang (Sakana AI, University of Michigan, and Institute of Science Tokyo) train a 0.6B coordinator that learns to delegate each turn of a query to one of seven larger LLMs and assign it a role, instead of answering the query itself.

Combining diverse foundation models is promising, but weight-merging is limited by mismatched architectures and closed APIs. Trinity addresses this with a lightweight coordinator that orchestrates collaboration among large language models (LLMs). The coordinator, comprising a compact language model (approximately B parameters) and a lightweight head (approximately K parameters), is optimized with an evolutionary strategy for efficient and adaptive delegation. Trinity processes queries over multiple turns, where at each turn the coordinator assigns one of three roles (Thinker, Worker, or Verifier) to a selected LLM, effectively offloading complex skill acquisition from the coordinator itself. Experiments show that Trinity consistently outperforms individual models and existing methods across coding, math, reasoning, and domain knowledge tasks, and generalizes robustly to out-of-distribution tasks. On standard benchmarks, Trinity achieves state-of-the-art results, including a score of 86.2% on LiveCodeBench. Theoretical and empirical analyses identify two main factors behind this performance: (1) the coordinator’s hidden-state representations provide rich contextualization of inputs, and (2) under high dimensionality and strict budget constraints, the separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy offers advantages over reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and random search by exploiting potential block--separability.

Methods

The contribution is a small, cheap-to-train coordinator placed in front of a pool of larger models, deciding who does what each turn. The harder problem is how to train it, because the right decision has no labels. The paper rules out supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in turn, then trains the coordinator with a black-box evolution strategy.

The coordinator

  • A 0.6B coordinator with a ~10K-parameter head. Two pieces are trained on top of a frozen Qwen3-0.6B small language model (SLM):
    • The selection head. A lightweight head (~10K parameters) runs beside the SLM’s usual language-model head. At each turn it reads the hidden state at the penultimate output-token position and emits two sets of logits: one selects an LLM from the pool, the other assigns it a role.
    • Singular value fine-tuning (SVF). The other trained piece rescales the singular values of the SLM’s weight matrices, leaving the rest of the base model frozen. SVF is carried over from the same group’s earlier Transformer-Squared [2], which adapts a model by rescaling existing singular values rather than adding new parameters. Transformer² trained those scales with reinforcement learning. Trinity keeps the parametrization but swaps in an evolution strategy, for the reasons in the next section.
  • Three roles, assigned per turn. A query runs over up to five turns. On each turn the chosen LLM is cast as a Thinker (decompose the problem), a Worker (perform a step), or a Verifier (check the running answer and flag edge cases), and a message-processing module injects the matching role prompt before the call. Figure 1 walks through a depreciation problem: a Thinker decomposes it on turn 1, a Worker computes on turn 2, a Verifier checks the result on turn 3.
  • A linear head is enough, because the representation is already separable. A linear SVM sorts the SLM’s penultimate-token hidden states into the four task types at 100%, far above the 25% chance line (Figure 5). With the representation that well-structured, a small linear head has enough signal to read off coordination decisions.

Why an evolution strategy, not RL or SFT

This is the paper’s central design choice. The coordinator’s target, which LLM to call and which role to assign each turn, has no ground truth. The only signal is a binary pass/fail reward earned by running the full multi-turn pipeline end to end, so there is nothing to fit with supervised learning directly. The paper works through the alternatives:

  • Synthetic labels plus SFT: ruled out by cost. One option is to manufacture labels, running the whole pool on each question and taking the per-question-best model, then fine-tuning on them. That is feasible for a single step but explodes in the multi-turn setting (up to five turns, seven models, three roles), where the paper estimates label generation at roughly LLM calls.
  • Reinforcement learning: ruled out by low-signal gradients. REINFORCE is the natural label-free optimizer, but the ~10K parameters are weakly coupled, so each one barely moves the scalar reward. Under a binary reward and a tight budget its per-parameter gradients are too low-signal to learn from, and random search does worse, collapsing onto a single agent and role.
  • The choice: separable CMA-ES. SVF fixes which parameters move, the singular-value scales plus the head. The optimizer is how they move: Trinity searches that parameter vector with the separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (sep-CMA-ES), keeping a Gaussian over the parameters, sampling candidate vectors, scoring each by running the coordinator, and shifting the Gaussian toward the ones that scored better. It needs no labels and no gradient, and because it ranks whole parameter vectors instead of estimating a per-parameter gradient, it sidesteps the exact low-signal problem that makes REINFORCE ineffective here.
    • Block--separability lets the cheap diagonal variant suffice. The paper argues the objective splits into near-independent blocks, one per agent and role choice, that interact only weakly. The in the name bounds how much residual coupling remains across blocks. When that coupling is small, a diagonal covariance gives up almost nothing against a full one, so the cheap sep-CMA-ES matches a full-covariance search that would cost .

The ablation in the Results section makes the choice concrete: at matched budget, sep-CMA-ES clears the REINFORCE, random-search, and SFT baselines on every in-distribution task.

Results

Trinity coordinates a pool of seven LLMs: three closed (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet) and four open (Gemma 3 27B-IT, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B in direct and reasoning modes). It is trained and evaluated on four in-distribution tasks (MATH500 [3], MMLU [4], RLPR [5], and LiveCodeBench [6]) and tested zero-shot on four held-out tasks (AIME 2025 [7], BigCodeBench [8], MT-Bench [9], and GPQA-Diamond [10]). The baselines:

  • each single model at its base budget and at a 5× context budget
  • single-model five-turn self-reflection
  • multi-agent methods: Mixture-of-Agents, RouterDC, and Smoothie

A per-question-best oracle (the union of correct answers across all seven models) marks the ceiling no coordinator over this pool can pass.

  • Beats every single model and multi-agent baseline in-distribution. On the four training tasks Trinity tops all baselines (Figure 3, the cover) and comes close to the per-question-best oracle on MATH500 (0.88 against 0.91), MMLU (0.92 against 0.97), and LiveCodeBench (0.61 against 0.65). The gap to the oracle is widest on RLPR (0.41 against 0.61) [1].
  • Generalizes zero-shot to held-out tasks. Averaged over the four held-out tasks (Table 1), Trinity scores 54.21, ahead of the strongest single models Gemini 2.5 Pro (52.34) and GPT-5 (51.07). It takes the top spot on AIME (50.00), MT-Bench (9.60), and GPQA-Diamond (76.82), and ties for first on BigCodeBench (35.80) [1].
  • Sets a LiveCodeBench record unconstrained. In the unconstrained setting (Figure 4), Trinity reaches a pass@1 of 86.2% on LiveCodeBench V6 (newly released questions spanning January to April 2025), a new state of the art, and the score rises with the per-query turn budget.
  • Every component contributes to the score. An ablation on the in-distribution tasks removes one piece at a time (Table 2): dropping the singular-value fine-tuning, the Thinker role, the tri-role selection, or the penultimate-token readout each lowers Trinity’s average, and Trinity outscores all three closed single models head-to-head [1].

My Notes

  • The evolution strategy beats their RL baseline at matched budget. Trinity’s optimizer comparison runs the same coordinator under four training methods at matched budget: REINFORCE scores 0.25 on LiveCodeBench and 0.46 on MATH500, while sep-CMA-ES reaches 0.62 and 0.88 [1]. That ordering matches a long-standing finding that evolution strategies stay competitive with policy-gradient reinforcement learning when the reward is sparse or binary [11]. It fits the regime here: a high-dimensional search over ~10K weakly coupled parameters, where REINFORCE’s per-parameter gradients are too low-signal to learn from, against a pass/fail task reward. Sakana ships this evolution-trained coordinator as Sakana Fugu [12], the everyday model in the product’s two-model line: Fugu builds on Trinity, while the heavier Fugu-Ultra builds on the RL-trained Conductor [15]. The two are separate models behind one endpoint rather than two stages of one orchestrator.
  • The 0.6B coordinator adds almost no capability of its own. It trains only the ~10K head and freezes the base model, so the answer quality comes from the frontier models it calls. Trinity therefore cannot beat the per-question-best oracle, the best any single model in the pool already gets right. It applies the routing idea behind a cost-routing triager to quality, and has the same limitation: it helps only when a capable model is already in the pool.
  • The coordinator builds the agentic graph dynamically, turn by turn. Choosing an LLM and a role at each turn is the same as constructing the multi-agent topology on the fly: every step adds the next node for that specific query, rather than running a structure fixed in advance. Trinity is one of several recent systems that learn this structure rather than hand-build it: MASS searches prompts and topologies offline into a fixed design [13], MAPO trains a policy for when to defer [14], and Sakana’s own pair builds it online, by reinforcement learning in Conductor [15] and by an evolution strategy here, then ships both behind one endpoint in Sakana Fugu [12].

item.title: Transformer²: Self-Adaptive LLMs
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Transformer²: Self-Adaptive LLMs [1] (ICLR 2025), Qi Sun, Edoardo Cetin, and Yujin Tang (Sakana AI and Institute of Science Tokyo) introduce a self-adaptation framework that fine-tunes only the singular values of a model’s weights into reusable expert vectors, then mixes them at inference to specialize the model per prompt.

Self-adaptive large language models (LLMs) aim to solve the challenges posed by traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often computationally intensive and static in their ability to handle diverse tasks. We introduce Transformer-Squared, a novel self-adaptation framework that adapts LLMs for unseen tasks in real-time by selectively adjusting only the singular components of their weight matrices. During inference, Transformer-Squared employs a two-pass mechanism: first, a dispatch system identifies the task properties, and then task-specific ‘expert’ vectors, trained using reinforcement learning, are dynamically mixed to obtain targeted behavior for the incoming prompt. Our method consistently outperforms ubiquitous approaches such as LoRA, with fewer parameters and greater efficiency. Furthermore, Transformer-Squared demonstrates versatility across different LLM architectures and modalities, including vision-language tasks. Transformer-Squared represents a significant leap forward, offering a scalable, efficient solution for enhancing the adaptability and task-specific performance of LLMs, paving the way for truly dynamic, self-organizing AI systems.

Methods

The framework has two parts: a parameter-efficient way to build task experts, and a two-pass scheme to deploy them at inference.

  • Singular value fine-tuning (SVF). Take the singular value decomposition of each weight matrix, , and learn a small vector that rescales the singular values, giving . Only is trained (one scalar per singular value), so the directions stay frozen and the parameter count is a fraction of LoRA’s per matrix. SVF is trained with reinforcement learning on the task reward, which lets it learn from datasets that give only a final answer (for example GSM8K [2], where there is no explanatory text for next-token fine-tuning to imitate).
  • Expert vectors, one per domain. Running SVF on each training domain (math, coding, reasoning, vision-language) yields a set of compact “expert” vectors , each specializing the base model toward one capability.
  • Two-pass inference. On a new prompt, the first pass classifies the task and the second pass applies the matching expert (or a mix of experts) to the frozen base weights, then generates the answer. The paper gives three dispatch strategies: a prompt-based classifier, a trained classification expert, and a few-shot mixture that blends experts by learned weights. An explicit “others” category falls back to the unmodified base model when no expert fits.

Results

The paper evaluates SVF and the full Transformer² framework on three base models across different families and sizes (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama3-70B-Instruct), on math (GSM8K), coding (MBPP-Pro [3]), and reasoning (ARC-Easy [4]), plus a vision-language setting (TextVQA [5]). The main baseline is LoRA [6], trained on the same domains, and scores in parentheses are normalized to the base model.

Trained on domain-specific data, SVF matches or beats LoRA on nearly every model and task while training orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and it avoids the degradations LoRA sometimes shows, most visibly on Llama3-70B, where LoRA drops below the base model on math and coding while SVF holds or improves.

Fine-tuning results on the test splits of math, coding, and reasoning, best per base model in bold. SVF matches or beats LoRA in most rows, and on Llama3-70B LoRA degrades the base model while SVF does not. Table 1 from the paper [1].
Method GSM8K MBPP-Pro ARC-Easy
Llama3-8B-Instruct 75.89 64.65 88.59
+ LoRA 77.18 67.68 88.97
+ SVF 79.15 66.67 89.56
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 42.83 49.50 81.65
+ LoRA 44.66 51.52 81.19
+ SVF 49.74 51.52 85.14
Llama3-70B-Instruct 85.29 80.81 89.10
+ LoRA 77.26 68.69 88.55
+ SVF 88.32 80.81 88.47

The expert vectors also recombine: a two-pass run on unseen tasks transfers gains, SVF experts trained on one model can be reused on another, and applying SVF to a vision-language backbone lifts the base model by over 39%.

My Notes

  • The technique TRINITY reuses, minus the RL. Transformer²’s SVF is the same singular-value rescaling that the same group later trains TRINITY [7]’s coordinator with. The lineage inverts one choice: here the expert vectors are learned with reinforcement learning, while TRINITY argues RL’s per-parameter gradients are too low-signal in its tight-budget regime and switches to an evolution strategy over the same SVF parameters.
  • Cheaper than LoRA because it rescales instead of adds. LoRA [6] adds a trainable low-rank matrix of parameters per weight, whereas SVF only scales the singular values that are already there. That is a much smaller, more constrained edit, and the constraint appears to help rather than hurt: it cannot introduce off-basis directions, which is likely why SVF avoids the base-model regressions LoRA shows on Llama3-70B.
  • RL on the reward sidesteps LoRA’s data requirement. Because SVF is trained against the task reward rather than by next-token imitation, it learns from answer-only datasets where LoRA needs explanatory text to imitate. This is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards applied at the fine-tuning layer: when the signal is correctness, you can optimize for it directly instead of for a proxy.

item.title: A Primer on the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES)
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

CMA-ES, the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy [1], [2], is a derivative-free optimizer for continuous problems: minimize over ( the number of variables), when you have no gradient because is a black box, non-differentiable, noisy, or simply cheaper to probe than to differentiate. It is the method of choice when you can afford a few thousand function evaluations but can’t backpropagate through them, and has long been a standard baseline in black-box and hyperparameter optimization. A recent example in machine learning is TRINITY [4], whose 0.6B LLM coordinator is trained with the diagonal sep-CMA-ES variant.

Intuition

Picture finding the deepest part of a murky lake with nothing but a fishing line and a heavy sinker. From your boat’s current spot, you drop the line at a handful of places scattered around you, keep the few that came back deepest, and row toward them. If those deep spots line up in one direction, say a channel running northeast, you spread your next drops more along that direction and less across it, and bunch them in a tighter cluster as the depths stop improving, since by then the deepest spot is right around you and only precision is left to gain. CMA-ES is that procedure made precise.

The name CMA-ES has two halves, and so does the method. The evolution strategy is the loop you just ran on the lake: each round spawns a population of candidate guesses, keeps the best few, and builds the next round’s guesses from them. This is search by selection rather than by gradient, repeated over generations, which places CMA-ES in the broader family of evolutionary algorithms. The covariance matrix adaptation is what makes the loop smart: rather than scattering the next guesses the same way every time, it learns the shape and spread of the region the best ones came from.

Underneath, the search keeps a cloud of guesses: densest where it is most hopeful, thinning toward the edges. The only things it remembers from one round to the next are where to aim that cloud and how the cloud is spread around the aim point. CMA-ES uses one particular cloud shape, the multivariate Gaussian (the many-dimensional cousin of the bell curve), and a few plain reasons make it the right choice:

  • A center and a spread, nothing more: those two are all the method tracks, and a bell-shaped cloud is exactly the shape they describe. Any other shape would smuggle in detail the method never measured (this is the maximum-entropy principle: given a mean and covariance, the Gaussian is the least-committal distribution).
  • Its spread is an oval you can stretch and tilt: the cloud need not be a round blob. It can run long and thin in one direction and tilt to any angle, which is just what you want once the deep spots reveal a channel to follow.
  • It ignores how the map is oriented: rotate or stretch the lake map and the cloud is still the same kind of cloud, so the search does equally well no matter which way you happened to call north.
  • It is easy to work with: drawing guesses from a bell-shaped cloud is quick, and the rules for sliding its center and reshaping its oval always leave a sensible cloud behind.

The one catch: a bell-shaped cloud has a single hump, so the search works one basin at a time. If the lake has two deep holes far apart, it settles into whichever one it drifts into. The usual fix is not a fancier cloud but re-running the search from a few random starting spots and keeping the best result.

The core idea

Formally, that cloud is a multivariate Gaussian, and each round repeats three steps: sample a population of candidates from it, evaluate on each, then move and reshape the Gaussian toward the candidates that did best. Over generations the mean drifts toward the optimum and the shape stretches to match the local curvature of the objective. The whole algorithm is just how you update that Gaussian.

The distribution has three parts:

  • is the mean, the current best guess at the optimum.
  • is the covariance matrix, the shape and orientation of the search ellipsoid (the three panels in the figure above).
  • is the step size, an overall scale factor held separate from so the algorithm can grow or shrink the whole search without relearning its shape.

One generation, step by step

The weights set an effective sample size , the recurring “how many points am I really averaging” quantity. The weights themselves are a fixed log-rank recipe (best gets the most, declining with rank), set once from rather than learned. The quantities CMA-ES actually adapts are the cloud’s covariance and step size , handled in the next two steps.

Adapt the covariance. is nudged to make the steps that just succeeded more likely next time, through two complementary terms:

Here and are small fixed learning rates for the rank-one and rank- terms, and retains the rest of the old , so the update is exponential smoothing: it folds a little new evidence into the matrix each round. The rank-one term uses an evolution path , the search’s momentum: an exponentially-weighted accumulation of successive mean shifts that grows long when the mean keeps heading one way and stays short when the steps cancel. The rate sets how fast the path forgets old steps:

The coefficient is just a normalization constant: it holds at unit scale when successive steps point in random directions, so the path’s length is informative. (The factor is the variance-preserving weight that pairs with the decay, and the undoes the shrinkage from averaging points.) When the mean keeps moving the same way generation after generation, those steps add up and stretches along that ridge. This is where CMA-ES picks up correlations between coordinates over time that one generation’s small sample is too noisy to estimate. The rank- term, by contrast, works within the current generation: it is the empirical covariance of this round’s successful steps, the shape of the cloud of good points estimated in one shot.

Adapt the step size. Separately, a second, conjugate evolution path (with its own decay rate ) tracks step direction after each step is rescaled by to undo the cloud’s shape, turning the oval back into a round, unit-spread blob (the whitening transform). The step size then grows or shrinks by comparing that path’s length to how long it would be if successive steps were uncorrelated:

Here is the same kind of normalization constant as , is a damping constant that keeps each change to small, and is the expected length of a random step under no selection (about ). The logic: if consecutive steps point the same way, the accumulated path is longer than random selection would produce, so you are making consistent progress and take bigger steps. If they zig-zag and cancel, the path is short, you are overshooting, and the step size shrinks. Splitting this off from decouples “how far to move” from “which directions matter,” and is most of why CMA-ES tunes itself with almost no hand-set hyperparameters. What adapting the covariance buys

Near a smooth optimum , looks quadratic: , with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives). By driving toward , CMA-ES learns the local shape from rank information alone, a derivative-free, stochastic cousin of quasi-Newton methods. That adaptive shape is the whole advantage: it makes the search invariant to rotation and lets it handle ill-conditioned objectives (long narrow valleys) that round, same-in-every-direction methods like random search or hill-climbing crawl through. It is also the cost: with free parameters and an update rate of about , is the slow, expensive part of the algorithm. CMA-ES trades speed for the flexibility of a non-spherical search shape.

sep-CMA-ES: the diagonal variant

A full costs memory and needs a periodic eigendecomposition to form and . That is fine for up to a few hundred, painful in the thousands, and hopeless at and beyond. With free parameters and rates , a full is also slow to learn, a problem when the evaluation budget is tight.

sep-CMA-ES [3] restricts to be diagonal, learning one variance per coordinate and discarding all cross-coordinate correlations:

That drops memory and per-step cost to (the matrix square roots become element-wise, with no eigendecomposition), and because there are now only free parameters, the covariance learning rate can be raised, so it converges in far fewer evaluations. Geometrically, it can stretch the search ellipsoid along the coordinate axes (the middle panel of the cover figure) but cannot rotate it (the right panel). The price is the lost correlations: sep-CMA-ES assumes the problem is close to axis-aligned. When coordinates interact strongly, dropping the off-diagonal terms can stall the search where full CMA-ES would not.

That trade-off is exactly why TRINITY [4] reaches for sep-CMA-ES rather than the full algorithm: its coordinator is a roughly 10K-dimensional search under a tight evaluation budget, where a full covariance is both too expensive and too slow to learn, and the paper argues the objective is near-separable enough (it calls this block--separability) for the diagonal approximation to hold.

When to reach for CMA-ES

CMA-ES fits a specific regime: a continuous problem of low-to-moderate dimension where you can score a candidate but have no usable gradient, because the objective is non-differentiable, noisy, or a black box. Where a gradient is available, gradient descent through backpropagation is almost always faster and scales to millions of parameters, and CMA-ES does not try to compete there.

Its closest relatives are the gradient-free reinforcement-learning methods. Like policy-gradient RL, CMA-ES searches by trial and reward rather than by differentiating the objective. The difference is that policy gradients still need a low-variance gradient estimate to be useful, while CMA-ES needs only the ranking of scores, which keeps it working when the reward is sparse or binary [5]. The dividing line is dimensionality and structure: a full covariance is practical only up to the hundreds to low thousands of variables, which is what pushes larger problems toward the diagonal sep-CMA-ES variant or back toward reinforcement learning.

  2. Hansen, N. and Ostermeier, A. “Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies.” Evolutionary Computation 9(2): 159–195, 2001. https://doi.org/10.1162/106365601750190398
  3. Ros, R. and Hansen, N. “A Simple Modification in CMA-ES Achieving Linear Time and Space Complexity.” Parallel Problem Solving from Nature (PPSN X), LNCS 5199, pp. 296–305, Springer, 2008. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-87700-4_30
  4. Xu, Jinglue, Sun, Qi, Schwendeman, Peter, Nielsen, Stefan, Cetin, Edoardo, and Tang, Yujin. “TRINITY: An Evolved LLM Coordinator.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026. arXiv:2512.04695, December 4, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04695

item.title: The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Last August, Erik Brynjolfsson and his Stanford team found a sharp employment decline for the most AI-exposed workers aged 22 to 25. Fortune reports that he has since turned the one-off finding into a live instrument: the Canaries Dashboard, built with ADP Research on payroll data covering roughly one in six American workers, extends the series to April 2026 and shows the effect has not mean-reverted.

The dashboard draws on ADP payroll records covering 4.6 million workers across more than 730 occupations, and operationalizes the October 2025 paper Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence by Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen. A note on the early-career numbers below, which slice the data three ways: the cover’s 2.5% is the April 2026 decline for workers aged 22 to 25 across all occupations pooled, the cover’s 4.2% is that same cohort in the most AI-exposed occupations at that date, and the 3.8% cited in the text is the most-exposed cohort’s year-over-year decline averaged over the full series. What the dashboard reports:

  • The age cut, not the aggregate. Across all workers the effect is muted: AI-exposed occupations grew 1.1% a year since ChatGPT against 2% for the least-exposed, and contracted just 0.2% year over year as of April 2026. The divergence is by career stage. Workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations are shrinking 3.8% a year while the least-exposed in that cohort grow 2%. The early-career decline sharpened from a 2.8% drop to April 2024 to more than 4% a year since. Mid-career workers aged 31 to 34 are also down 1.7%, while those aged 35 to 40 grow at 2%.
  • The effect is concentrated in specific high-exposure jobs. Software developers sit in the most-exposed occupation group: early-career workers (22-25) show large declines while older cohorts keep expanding. Customer service representatives, also highly exposed, follow the same shape, with declines in the two youngest groups and growth for the rest.
  • Low-exposure work shows no such age gradient. In occupations AI barely touches, employment trends have little relationship to age. Stock clerks fall across the board, and home health aides, among the least exposed under most frameworks, actually show early-career workers gaining more than older groups.
  • The trend persists, and survives the obvious controls. The original paper ran through August 2025. The dashboard extends it to April 2026, with the effect growing about half a percentage point per month rather than reverting. Brynjolfsson reports removing the entire tech sector, isolating remote-work effects, and noting that the most rate-sensitive occupations like construction have the lowest AI exposure, so the interest-rate explanation points the wrong way.
  • The mechanism, per Richardson. Nela Richardson describes it as AI absorbing tasks from the bottom up rather than jobs from the top down. Occupations where AI augments human work show more enduring growth than those where it automates tasks outright. The dashboard already shows the effect in software development and customer service, and its absence in low-exposure work like home health care.

Related Posts

  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: the skeptic on the other side of this debate, who reads the same labor data with far lower productivity estimates.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the displacement debate in miniature, the same mechanism read once as imminent crisis and once as overstated, which this dashboard’s persistence speaks to directly.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: a parallel empirical instrument measuring AI’s labor impact, tracking task speedup and deskilling where this one tracks employment by age.
  • Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?: a roundtable on which jobs are most exposed and what to tell young workers, the people this dashboard’s early-career decline lands on.
  • MSR: Which Occupations GenAI Is Actually Used In: pairs measured real-world usage with this dashboard’s measured employment effect, both moving past projected exposure.

item.title: How Far Behind the Closed Frontier Are Open-Weights LLMs?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In a Doubleword post, Jamie Dborin takes a plot making the rounds on Twitter (durable version), which shows the shrinking gap between open-weights and closed-source LLMs, and re-runs it across every benchmark Artificial Analysis publishes to test whether the open-weights frontier is really about to catch up.

What the post reports:

  • The gap is measured as a time lag: how many months back the closed-source frontier sat at the level the open-weights frontier reaches today.
  • On the headline Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the gap has shrunk reliably since around summer 2024. A line of best fit hits zero around December 3, 2026, roughly six months after the post was written.
  • That is one benchmark. Repeating the analysis across all 18 benchmarks Artificial Analysis tracks, the average gap is almost flat, just under five months for the whole period, and looks like it may be growing on most datasets.
  • Coding is the exception: its gap fell from about 15 months behind to one or two, which accounts for much of the apparent convergence.

My Notes

  • Months behind is not a clean catch-up estimate: it describes the past rather than the future. Let and be the closed and open frontier performance at time , improving at rates and . The plot’s lag is defined by , so and The denominator is the closed frontier’s rate, so a falling can mean the gap shrank (open catching up) or that rose (closed accelerating). The forward question, when open weights actually reach the closed frontier, divides the same gap by the rate difference instead: which is positive only when : open weights catch up only by improving faster than the closed frontier, not merely by improving. When the average is flat, as in the article’s ~5-month figure, , so the gap holds rather than closes and runs to infinity even while “months behind” stays comfortably small.

  • Coding drives the convergence and is the weakest evidence for it: the apparent catch-up is mostly coding, whose lag fell from about 15 months to one or two. A small time lag is not the same as a small point gap, though. In today’s ranking points the Artificial Analysis methodology post still puts coding among the widest open-versus-closed gaps. Two further reasons to discount the coding result:

    • Optimized and contamination-prone: coding is the capability open-weights labs invest in most heavily, and coding benchmarks are a known contamination risk. LiveCodeBench, one of the eighteen benchmarks here, exists to give a contamination-free code evaluation by pulling fresh contest problems after a cutoff date, the same post-cutoff defense the Leipzig math benchmark used.
    • Harness may compress the gap (speculative): Artificial Analysis runs every model through the same open-source agentic harness (an E2B sandbox, a fixed tool set, up to 250 turns), so the harness is controlled. But the harness does much of the work, and a forgiving one can let a weaker model reach similar end-to-end task outcomes, which may reduce the measured gap.

Related Posts

  • How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index: documents the weighting and scoring of the benchmark suite this analysis runs on, and measures the same gap in current ranking points rather than months of lag.
  • Benchmarks in Leipzig: a contamination-resistant math benchmark built from post-cutoff unpublished questions, the defense the public coding benchmarks here lack.
  • Mapping Global Dynamics of Benchmark Creation and Saturation in AI: how benchmarks saturate over time, the backdrop to why a single index can show convergence that a wider set does not.

item.title: From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting [1] (arXiv preprint, June 2026), Catarina G. Belém, Shang Wu, Hongyu Yao, Mark Steyvers, Sameer Singh, and Padhraic Smyth (UC Irvine + MIT) show that when language models paraphrase, simplify, or summarize scientific and medical text, they tend to strengthen how confidently a claim is stated even while keeping its meaning intact, turning a hedged “may” into a flat “is.”

Humans increasingly turn to Language Models (LMs) in ways that shape beliefs and drive decisions, including discussing, rewriting, and summarizing information from scientific articles, news, and medical reports. However, in these domains, where how confidently a claim is expressed matters, little is known about whether LMs faithfully preserve it. In this work, we investigate certainty distortion in LMs, defined as meaningful changes in expressed certainty when semantic content is preserved. We propose an LM-based evaluation metric that is consistent with population-level judgments of certainty. Using this metric, we characterize certainty distortion across different sizes and families of models in the context of scientific and medical communication tasks. Our results show that certainty distortion affects up to 75% of LM outputs and is systematically asymmetric in rewriting tasks with most LMs being 1.5-2× more likely to increase the expressed certainty than to decrease it. These effects can compound over repeated paraphrasing: in the medical domain, claude-haiku-4-5 increases certainty of 20% examples after a single iteration, increasing to 40% after five iterations. Prompt-based interventions reduce overall certainty distortion but do not eliminate it. Together, these findings reveal a general bias toward inflating expressed certainty, with direct implications for users who rely on LMs in high-stakes domains.

Methods

The paper defines certainty distortion (CD) as a genuine change in how confidently a claim is expressed when the meaning is held fixed, and splits it by direction: CD-↑ is inflation (the rewrite is judged more certain than the source) and CD-↓ is deflation (less certain). The hard part is measuring a subjective property at scale, since perceived certainty is a matter of human judgment rather than a fact with an answer key. The metric the paper proposes is an LM-as-judge comparison:

  • The judge () sees the original text and the rewrite, presented anonymously as Text A and Text B to avoid an order or label bias.
  • It picks which one communicates the main finding with greater certainty on a 5-point scale (Clearly A, A, No clear difference, B, Clearly B), mapped to .
  • A clear shift away from zero counts as distortion, signed for direction.

To check that the judge stands in for a reader, the authors run a human study and measure each annotator’s agreement with the population consensus (the leave-one-out mean of the other annotators) using the Kendall rank correlation. The LM judge tracks the consensus better than the average individual annotator does ( versus ), and beats a prior BERT-based certainty estimator (, a gap of in its favor). A judge that matches the human consensus more closely than individual humans match each other is a counterintuitive result, and part of it comes from how the consensus is computed rather than from the judge being genuinely better, so Figure 2 looks more favorable to the judge than a like-for-like comparison would. I come back to this in a note below.

Results

The evaluation covers two domains and four content-preserving tasks: paraphrasing, news-style rewriting, simplification, and summarization. In each case a model produces one of these rewrites from a source text, and the judge then compares its output against the original:

  • Science: SPICED [2], a dataset of single-sentence scientific findings, each paired with a news and a social-media version. The model rewrites the finding itself, either paraphrasing it or recasting it as a New York Times sentence. The paper uses the finding as the source and keeps only those whose paired news version conveys the same information, scoring at least 4 on SPICED’s information matching score (an averaged human 1-to-5 rating of whether two texts state the same finding). A new set of 500 academic abstracts across five social- and life-science disciplines adds a document-level summarization task.
  • Medicine: the Findings sections of 800 MIMIC-CXR [3] radiology reports, kept only when they contain at least one hedged sentence so there is certainty to lose, where models either paraphrase or simplify the text.

Five instruction-tuned models are tested: Gemini 3.1 (fl), GPT-5-nano, and Claude Haiku 4.5 as closed models, and Llama 3.3 (70B) and Qwen3 (8B) as open ones. Every output is scored with the validated LM-as-judge metric, and semantic-similarity checks confirm the rewrites preserve meaning.

The main findings:

  • Distortion is common. Across tasks, average CD ranges from 30.0% (GPT-5-nano) to 49.4% (Llama 3.3 70B), and the worst single setting reaches roughly 75% (Claude Haiku 4.5 at 74.8% and Gemini 3.1 at 75.3% on news rewriting).
  • The errors point one way. In four of the five models, inflation outpaces deflation. The obvious confound is where the source starts: a text already stated with high certainty has little room to be inflated (a ceiling) and a very tentative one little room to be deflated (a floor), which on its own would produce a directional skew. Splitting the results by source certainty (low, medium, high) confirms that floor/ceiling pattern, but the magnitudes stay asymmetric, with models inflating uncertain sources more often than they deflate certain ones, so the bias is not just an artifact of the starting point.
  • It builds up in medicine. When a model rewrites its own output for up to five turns, scientific text mostly settles after the first rewrite, but radiology reports keep drifting upward: Claude Haiku 4.5 inflates 20% of examples after one turn and 40% after five.
  • Scale, temperature, and prompting each help only partly.
    • Scale: larger models within a family distort somewhat less but still substantially (46.1–70% on SPICED, 19–27.4% on MIMIC). On news rewriting, distortion falls from 74.8% to 55.7% across the Claude family while the GPT family barely moves (44.3% to 46.1%).
    • Temperature: no significant effect for most models.
    • Prompting: stacking three constraints lowers paraphrase CD from 50.6% to 40.1% and news CD from 64.3% to 41.9%, but only an explicit instruction to preserve the original certainty comes close to removing the directional bias.

The ratio (column R) makes the asymmetry concrete: it is the inflation rate divided by the deflation rate (CD-↑ over CD-↓), so a value above 1 means a model strengthens certainty more often than it weakens it. Most models fall between 1.5 and 2.0, meaning they raise certainty 1.5 to 2 times as often as they lower it. Llama 3.3 is the exception, roughly even on science and actually deflating more often than it inflates on medicine (0.6), which shows the bias is a tendency across current models rather than a universal law.

My Notes

  • A different question from self-calibration: most work on LM certainty asks whether a model’s stated confidence tracks its own accuracy, the verbalized-confidence line that runs from Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know [4] through Just Ask for Calibration [5]. This paper measures something else: whether a model preserves the certainty a source chose to express when it rewrites that source’s text. A model can be well calibrated about its own answers and still strip the hedges out of someone else’s.

  • The judge’s edge over humans is partly an artifact: the validation reports the LM judge correlating with the human consensus at against for the average annotator, but the two are scored against different targets. Each human is correlated against a leave-one-out consensus, the mean of the other annotators with itself removed, while the judge, never in the pool, is correlated against the full annotator mean. The fuller mean is a lower-variance target and spares the judge the self-exclusion penalty each human pays, so both effects favor the model. The paper’s own fair comparison is its pairwise metric, judge-to-human against human-to-human consistency (Appendix B), where the judge comes out comparable rather than better.

  • The asymmetry looks like preference tuning: the paper leaves the mechanism open. One candidate is preference optimization, which rewards direct, fluent, decisive phrasing. The same pressure shows up as overconfidence in verbalized probabilities after human-feedback fine-tuning [5] and as sycophancy toward whatever looks like the more assertive answer [6]. Hedges like “may,” “could,” and “suggests” are exactly the words a preference model learns to treat as less helpful, so a meaning-preserving rewrite quietly drops them. This is a hypothesis the results are consistent with, not something the paper tests.

  • Repeated rewrites strip out uncertainty: the broken-telephone result matters most where text is rewritten repeatedly with no human reading the intermediate steps, such as retrieval-augmented summaries, agent hand-offs, and multi-hop pipelines that paraphrase a paraphrase. Earlier broken-telephone studies tracked properties like toxicity, sentiment, and length. Certainty is more consequential because dropping a hedge changes a claim’s epistemic status, turning “may be secondary to COPD” into “is attributed to COPD” [1]. In the medical setting the drift did not saturate after one pass: Claude Haiku 4.5 doubled its inflation rate from 20% to 40% over five turns.

References

  1. Belém, Catarina G., Wu, Shang, Yao, Hongyu, Steyvers, Mark, Singh, Sameer, and Smyth, Padhraic. “From ‘May’ to ‘Is’: Certainty Distortion in Language Model Rewriting.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.07951), June 6, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07951

  2. Wright, Dustin, Pei, Jiaxin, Jurgens, David, and Augenstein, Isabelle. “Modeling Information Change in Science Communication with Semantically Matched Paraphrases.” EMNLP 2022 (arXiv:2210.13001), October 24, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13001

  3. Johnson, Alistair E. W., Pollard, Tom J., Berkowitz, Seth J., Greenbaum, Nathaniel R., Lungren, Matthew P., Deng, Chih-ying, Mark, Roger G., and Horng, Steven. “MIMIC-CXR, a de-identified publicly available database of chest radiographs with free-text reports.” Scientific Data 6:317, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0322-0

  4. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221

  5. Tian, K., Mitchell, E., Zhou, A., Sharma, A., Rafailov, R., Yao, H., Finn, C., and Manning, C. D. “Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback.” EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.14975), May 24, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14975

  6. Sharma, M., Tong, M., Korbak, T., et al. “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models.” ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.13548), October 20, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548

Related Posts

  • Just Ask for Calibration: human-feedback fine-tuning leaves models overconfident in the probabilities they state. The inflation bias here is that same overconfidence showing up when a model rewrites text rather than answers a question.
  • Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations: trains models to express calibrated uncertainty in their own words, the constructive flip side of faithfully preserving someone else’s expressed certainty.
  • SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: asks whether a model can put its own uncertainty into words, where this paper asks whether it preserves a source’s uncertainty across a rewrite.
  • Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models: a training-side remedy aimed at the same failure, getting models to communicate uncertainty more faithfully.

item.title: PaperTrail: A Claim-Evidence Interface for Grounding Provenance in LLM-based Scholarly Q&A
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In PaperTrail [1] (CHI 2026), Anna Martin-Boyle and Harmanpreet Kaur (University of Minnesota), with Cara Leckey and Martha Brown at NASA Langley Research Center, build an interface that decomposes both an LLM’s answer and its source papers into claims and evidence, and find that showing researchers this finer-grained provenance lowered their trust in the answers without changing how much they relied on them.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in scholarly question-answering (QA) systems to help researchers synthesize vast amounts of literature. However, these systems often produce subtle errors (e.g., unsupported claims, errors of omission), and current provenance mechanisms like source citations are not granular enough for the rigorous verification that scholarly domain requires. To address this, we introduce PaperTrail, a novel interface that decomposes both LLM answers and source documents into discrete claims and evidence, mapping them to reveal supported assertions, unsupported claims, and information omitted from the source texts. We evaluated PaperTrail in a within-subjects study with 26 researchers who performed two scholarly editing tasks using PaperTrail and a baseline interface. Our results show that PaperTrail significantly lowered participants’ trust compared to the baseline. However, this increased caution did not translate to behavioral changes, as people continued to rely on LLM-generated scholarly edits to avoid a cognitively burdensome task. We discuss the value of claim-evidence matching for understanding LLM trustworthiness in scholarly settings, and present design implications for cognition-friendly communication of provenance information.

Methods

PaperTrail’s backend turns both the source papers and the LLM’s answer into matched claim-evidence pairs through a three-stage pipeline, then the frontend renders the matches so a reader can see what is supported, what is unsupported, and what the answer left out:

  • Stage 1, paper-level extraction (offline). Each source paper is preprocessed into structured claims and supporting evidence.
  • Stage 2, answer-level extraction (real-time). The LLM’s generated answer is decomposed into its own claims and evidence as it is produced.
  • Stage 3, claim-evidence matching (real-time). Similarity search retrieves the candidate paper claims relevant to the question, and an LLM aligns the answer’s claims with them, marking each supported, unsupported, or an omission, plus an overall claim-coverage indicator.

The choice of method is fixed per step at design time, judged by whether a user query is available to guide relevance, whether the step runs offline or in real time, and how much text it must process. In the evaluated system, Stage 1 extracts paper claims with an LLM and attaches their evidence by similarity, Stage 2 decomposes the answer with an LLM, and Stage 3 does claim-level retrieval: similarity search over the corpus of individual paper claims pulls the candidates relevant to the question, and an LLM then aligns the answer’s claims with them. The paper calls Stage 3 RAG, but the unit retrieved is a single claim and the LLM only selects among the candidates, so nothing is generated.

The claim-extraction backend is validated offline by scoring its extracted claims against two reference datasets: SciClaimHunt [2], the development set (precision 0.69, recall 0.62, F1 0.65), and BioClaimDetect [3], a human-annotated out-of-distribution test of whether the pipeline generalizes (precision 0.63, recall 0.88, F1 0.73). The lower precision on BioClaimDetect comes from the pipeline splitting sentences into finer atomic claims than the human annotators did, which manual inspection confirmed were valid claims rather than extraction errors.

Results

The evaluation has two parts: an offline check that the backend extracts and matches claims well enough to trust, and a within-subjects user study with 26 researchers who completed two scholarly editing tasks, once with PaperTrail and once with a baseline that offers only sentence-level source highlighting. The study tracked three primary measures and two secondary ones, then ran Spearman correlations across them:

  • Trust (primary): subjective trust in the LLM, on the validated 1–7 TXAI (Trust in Explainable AI) scale [4], asked after each task.
  • Reliance (primary): a behavioral measure of how much of the LLM’s draft survived into the final text, computed as 1 minus the normalized token-level Levenshtein edit distance [5] between the draft and the participant’s final text. A value of 1 means no edits (full reliance), lower means more rewriting.
  • Confidence (primary): subjective confidence in the edits made and in the final text, averaged over two 1–7 items.
  • Usability (secondary): the SUPR-Q usability questionnaire [6].
  • Cognitive load (secondary): the raw NASA-TLX (Task Load Index) workload score [7].

The findings, by the paper’s result sections:

  • §6.1, primary measures: trust fell, reliance and confidence held. PaperTrail significantly lowered trust in the LLM’s answers (mean 4.22 to 3.68, p = .015, d = 0.44), the intended effect of laying out unsupported claims and omissions. Reliance barely moved (0.73 vs 0.75, p = .313), and confidence held (4.27 vs 4.05, p = .525). Readers grew more skeptical without accepting any less.
  • §6.2, secondary measures: usability dropped, effort did not. Perceived usability was significantly lower with PaperTrail (5.05 to 4.48, p = .026, d = 0.52), while self-reported cognitive load was flat (4.10 vs 4.12, p = .838) and behavioral effort showed no significant change in clicks (8.26 vs 12.47, p = .137) or messages (3.67 vs 4.08, p = .438). The finer provenance felt harder to use without measurably raising workload.
  • §6.3, correlation analysis: reliance decoupled from trust. In the baseline, reliance rose with trust (r = 0.57, p < .01) and usability (r = 0.60, p < .05), so people who trusted the system more leaned on it more. With PaperTrail, that coupling vanished: reliance no longer rose with trust. The trust-behavior gap shows up here as a broken correlation. More-educated participants also reported lower confidence with PaperTrail (r = -0.41, p < .05), a sign they were more sensitive to the provenance laid out for them.
  • The authors call this a trust-behavior gap, and they surmise why. Verifying claims is slow, deliberate work, and under load people fall back on fast, automatic acceptance, so a richer provenance display can feel like understanding without prompting an actual check. The most-cited barrier in participant feedback was time: the roughly 20-minute task plus slow system latency left no room to verify, and several participants said the time pressure made them lean on the LLM more rather than less. The authors’ reframe is from measuring trust to measuring trustworthiness, with claim-evidence matching offered as one such signal.

My Notes

  • The trust-behavior gap is partly the tool’s fault. It is also bad news for provenance-as-fix in general: a large literature assumes better explanations or citations will calibrate reliance, but here a strictly more informative display made people more skeptical without changing what they did. Some of that is human (automation bias under time pressure), but some is the design: PaperTrail flags which claims are unsupported or omitted without coupling those flags to a cheaper next action, no suggested fix, no prioritized list of what to check first, no one-click correction, so noticing a problem and resolving it still cost the reader the same. The authors half-concede this, proposing two fixes: adaptive provenance that adjusts detail by context, and progressive engagement that trains verification skill over time.

  • PaperTrail catches the two errors the companion schema paper flags most. Those are unsupported claims and omissions. That paper [8] catalogs how scholarly-QA answers go wrong, and PaperTrail decomposes both the answer and its sources into claims to flag exactly those. The two were released together but neither cites the other, so the pairing is mine: one names the failure modes, the other is built to catch them.

  • PaperTrail reuses ExpertQA’s grading primitive for reading. ExpertQA [9] split answers into claims paired with evidence so experts could grade attribution after the fact. PaperTrail runs the same decomposition in real time and puts it in front of the reader. The same claim-evidence unit works for both scoring and reading LLM answers, not just for benchmarking.

  • Omissions are what a citation checker misses. Source-citation tools verify that what was said is supported. PaperTrail also flags what the source contained but the answer dropped, the same recall-side failure that rubric-coverage benchmarks [10] measure. Putting omission detection in a live editing interface is the novel move, since omission is precisely the error a reader cannot catch by checking the citations that are present.
